title: The Lost Museum: A Mystery of Four Perspectives
subtitle: Junior Curators of Cambridge
fiction_disclaimer: All curator requests, mystery clues, awards and character dialogue are fiction. This is not an official Fitzwilliam Museum programme or a confirmed partnership.

location.name: The Fitzwilliam Museum
location.address: Trumpington Street, Cambridge CB2 1RB, United Kingdom
location.operational_caution: All school groups must pre-book. Do not place codes/stickers in galleries. Check galleries, adult supervision, access and museum conditions in advance.

learning_outcomes: Cite an observed object or museum label as evidence
Explain the perspectives offered and omitted by differing object types
Teach one area of expertise to peers
Draft a cautious inclusive exhibition interpretation

roles.collaborator: WorldQuest Demo Collaborator — simulated, not museum staff

story.opening: The museum has a fictional challenge for our Junior Curators: a draft introduction treats very different objects as one single story. Investigate real exhibits, share your expertise, and propose a better evidence-based introduction.
story.caveat: There is no claim that the real museum has written such a draft.

missions.name: Evidence Detectives
missions.location_hint: Find Nespawershefyt’s coffin set; check gallery/object availability with the teacher.
missions.source_fact: The official gallery page identifies the coffin set of Nespawershefyt, given in 1822, and other funerary objects.
missions.narrative: What can the object itself tell us?
missions.physical_instruction: Look up and inspect an approved coffin exhibit. Record two details you can actually see. Then find its museum label.
missions.question: Which claim is observation and which is inference?
examples: Observation example (only if actually seen): I can see painted decoration.
Unsupported inference: Everyone in ancient Egypt had a decorated coffin.
missions.expected_learning: Distinguish what is observed from what is inferred; single artifacts are not universal evidence.
hints: Start with a material, shape, or decoration.
Separate words on the label from your own observations.
missions.accessible_alternative: Use approved official museum object gallery images and accompanying descriptive text.

missions.name: Power and Memory
missions.location_hint: Find the large sarcophagus lid of Ramesses III; check display with the teacher.
missions.source_fact: The Fitzwilliam notes the seven-ton sarcophagus lid of Ramesses III, given by G. B. Belzoni in 1823.
missions.physical_instruction: Observe the sarcophagus lid and choose two visible features that make it prominent.
missions.question: How might a monumental royal object affect which stories survive or appear prominently? Cite your observations and acknowledge what you do not know.
examples: This suggests the person was memorialised prominently, because the object is monumental.
Do not infer that all ancient Egyptians were similarly represented.
missions.expected_learning: Understand objects as evidence for power and commemoration and recognise limits of representation.
hints: Ask who the object relates to.
What might this object not tell you about ordinary experiences?
missions.accessible_alternative: Use the museum’s official Gallery 20 page and audio description where available.

missions.name: Multiple Lives
missions.location_hint: Find two DIFFERENT categories among gallery pottery, jewellery, coins, sculpture, or funerary monuments.
missions.source_fact: Gallery 21 features Greek/Roman pottery, sculpture, jewellery, coins and funerary monuments in a chronological display.
missions.narrative: Can two kinds of objects tell different stories?
missions.physical_instruction: Pick two different categories of object and record what you see.
missions.question: What different historical questions might these object types help us answer?
examples: Coins may help us investigate trade, authority or imagery, depending on the specific coin.
Funerary monuments can tell us about remembrance but cannot represent everyone.
missions.expected_learning: Compare types of evidence used to understand different aspects of historical lives.
hints: Look for different object types, not two of the same thing.
Ask what each helps historians know, and what it cannot prove.
missions.accessible_alternative: Use approved gallery descriptions and image examples.

missions.name: Connections and Voices
missions.location_hint: Look for Rome / Ancient Sudan context and arrange the facilitator discussion; no unsupervised stranger interviews.
missions.source_fact: Official Gallery 24 describes Rome and Ancient Sudan objects and grave reliefs from Palmyra; a facsimile of the Dendera Zodiac is mentioned.
missions.narrative: Whose perspective is present, and whose is missing?
missions.physical_instruction: Identify two geographical or cultural terms represented in the approved gallery context and note one question the display leaves you with.
missions.question: Ask a PRE-ARRANGED WorldQuest contributor how to make an interpretation fair to people whose views may not appear on a museum label.
examples: Question: What additional evidence or community perspectives would help?
Record the adult response as a perspective, not a museum quotation or uncontested fact.
missions.expected_learning: Recognise the role of human knowledge, multiple perspectives and uncertainty in interpretation.
hints: Start with the gallery title and signs.
What is a question that only new evidence or human perspectives could help answer?
missions.accessible_alternative: Teacher-guided conversation with a clearly labelled simulated contributor transcript.

partner_interaction.demo_actor_label: SIMULATED WorldQuest contributor — not Fitzwilliam staff
questions: What is evidence, and what is interpretation?
Whose perspective might be absent, and what would help us know?
How can we honestly show uncertainty in a short label?
partner_interaction.fallback: Teacher guided conversation; sample transcript explicitly fictional and marked demo.

peer_teaching.peer_comprehension_prompt: Name one thing another expert observed and why it matters.
peer_teaching.completion_rule: Each perspective verified for the home group; group participants complete teach-back check; teacher can audit/override.

steps.title: Match each object to the perspective it helps investigate

steps.question: Which exhibition principle is appropriately cautious?

options.text: Every object tells us everything about every person who used it.
Objects provide different evidence; historical interpretations require context and multiple perspectives.

steps.prompt: In 2–3 sentences cite at least two objects, describe multiple perspectives, note an uncertainty and invite a visitor question.

before.question: Can one museum object tell us everything about a whole society?

after.question: Select the claim that can be directly observed from a painted artifact.
